A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LLaMA-Omni study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and relocated prompts and case-study material can be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original instruction-following evaluations, speech-quality and latency measurements, decoding-time comparisons, and response examples in Tables 1–4.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark results, expanded streaming comparisons, and human preference evaluations, including Figure 4 and Appendix C.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 moves speech encoding and adaptation outside the generation loop, avoiding repeated computation as written in v1. This is a limited inference-procedure correction; the architecture, training objectives, and two-stage training remain unchanged. The expanded vocoder description does not establish a new component.

E1.justification: Both versions use InstructS2S-200K for training and the same 199-instruction InstructS2S-Eval benchmark, covering speech-to-text and offline/streaming speech-to-speech instruction following. The additional comparisons and human evaluation do not introduce a new dataset, domain, or task.

E2.justification: Section 4.3 replaces VITS with Orca in both SALMONN and Qwen2-Audio speech-output baselines, substantively changing the evaluated systems. v2 also compares these cascades and SpeechGPT against LLaMA-Omni across streaming chunk sizes, whereas v1's chunk-size comparison includes only LLaMA-Omni.

E3.justification: Section 4.2 and Appendix A replace separate, explicitly anchored content/style scores with one composite GPT-4o score. ASR-CER and lagging-word metrics disappear, while words per second is added. New protocols include Orca word-chunk sweeps and pairwise human evaluation using 20 instructions and five participants per comparison.

E4.justification: The single-model chunk-size sensitivity study becomes a comparative analysis of quality, alignment, and speech rate versus latency across four systems (Figure 3 and Appendix C). The separate S2TIF-versus-S2SIF decoding-time analysis is removed. The gift-wrapping case study is retained in Appendix B, rather than newly added or deleted.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed details, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. v2 adds descriptive dataset statistics and human vote totals, without introducing uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: The main ChatGPT results are replaced under a changed rubric and revised speech-output baselines, so their higher scores are not directly comparable gains. LLaMA-Omni's reported offline ASR-WER changes from 11.61 to 10.82, and minimum latency from 226.13 to 236.18 ms; its UTMOS values are retained. v2 adds extensive streaming results and human votes, including 48 wins, 28 ties, and 24 losses against SALMONN + Orca for helpfulness.

T1.justification: Equations 1–5 and the mathematical descriptions of adaptation, cross-entropy training, CTC alignment, and collapsing are retained. No new theorem, proof, formal assumption, or substantive derivation appears.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion revise the advertised minimum latency from 226 to 236 ms. The central contributions remain simultaneous text/speech generation without transcription, InstructS2S-200K, and training within three days on four GPUs. Added end-to-end and speech-style wording emphasizes existing claims.

C2.justification: v1 interprets LLaMA-Omni as having the best speech-text alignment; v2 acknowledges that Orca cascades align better offline and attributes its shortfall to limited speech-decoder training data. v2 also explains streaming advantages through fewer word-boundary pauses and steadier speech rate. However, its claim that ASR-WER improves with larger chunks contradicts Table 4, where error increases from 9.84 to 10.71.

D1.justification: v2 adds dataset duration/length summaries, direct model and audio-demo links, an exact vocoder checkpoint link, and disclosure that latency is measured on one NVIDIA L40 GPU. It also explains the vocoder's duration prediction. The main training schedule and model hyperparameters remain unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 5 adds substantive positioning against Mini-Omni and Moshi, asserting distinctions in the base LLM, CTC alignment, and training cost, and adds AnyGPT. Streaming-TTS literature receives substantial new discussion, replacing earlier coverage of decoder-only streaming and duplex models. The Anonymous-to-Cho citation update concerns the same Speechworthy work.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is substantially rewritten around offline results, comparative streaming results, and human evaluation. The decoding-time subsection disappears, the case study moves to Appendix B, and prompts are consolidated in Appendix A. Results interpretation and related-work prose undergo substantial rewriting despite largely retained introductory and methodological text.

P2.justification: v2 restructures the main results table, adds a dataset-statistics table, introduces four-panel streaming plots and human-vote charts, and supplies expanded numerical tables in Appendix C. The standalone decoding-time table disappears, while the existing case table and model prompt relocate to appendices. These substantially change the presentation of evidence.

improvement.justification: v1's central streaming-quality claim lacked comparable streaming-baseline evaluation and human assessment. v2 substantially addresses that deficiency through Orca-based competitors, comparative latency-quality curves, and a small paired listening study (Sections 4.5–4.6 and Appendix C). These gains strengthen the paper's central evidence despite the coarser automatic scoring rubric, loss of the separate decoding-time comparison, and incorrect ASR-WER trend description.
